title: Weekly Top Five Articles: The Shortage of Presence
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley's weekly curated list this time circles one theme, the shortage of embodied presence and real connection. Each of the five items gets a short editorial gloss: Gill Partington on mimeo poetry and being boxed into our language, Zena Hitz on lust as entertainment in an inner theater, a King's College London study showing childhood loneliness does not self-correct, a study of working-class single men's resentment he reads as frustrated eros turning to grievance, and a study of how a father's scent helps infants synchronize their brains with strangers. His closing synthesis is that human connection pulls the self outward, and that without it people drift toward fantasy, complaint and resignation. The roundup is archived for its curatorial framing and the interpretive commentary on each source, while the linked pieces are expanded separately.
points: Hitz's definition of lust as reducing desire for communion to entertainment is paired with the claim that we owe each other a world where lust is difficult.
The loneliness study is read as evidence that isolated children need to be drawn into fellowship by others rather than left to repair bonds themselves.
Bradley frames male political grievance as frustrated eros, noting that the underlying data is correlational and excluded women.
The infant study is used to argue that children learn trust from the nearness and faithfulness of a present parent.
His synthesis is that those with deep attachments can tolerate desire, loneliness and conflict because relationships matter to them.
quotes: Zena Hitz believes lust “consists in the reduction of our desire for communion into a form of entertainment, a play in an inner theater, one where the actors take real blows and bleed real blood.

The insight is that the disconnected soul does not fix itself: the craving for intimacy, when deprived of actual friendships, folds further inward. Children need to be brought into fellowship by others.

The larger interpretive point here is that frustrated eros does not remain private: when men can neither love nor work, their frustration turns to grievance and seeks expression in politics and in what Rachael Robnett terms the “manosphere.
The insight for interpretation: We borrow from the security of nearness and faithfulness in order to open up to strangers. Through the body of the one who stays we learn the wider world.
Human connection pulls the self outward toward others: father’s body, friend at school, spouse, work community, even page that stains the hand with ink.
People with deep connection and attachment to others can tolerate desire, loneliness, and inter-personal conflicts because keeping relationships matters to all us.
Gill Partington makes the important point that “thanks to the mimeo revolution . . . for the price of a few reams of paper and a handful of stencils” a poet could produce his or her own magazine.
